title: 8 words that look like cognates but aren’t
summary: The similarities between the English word “much” and the Spanish word “mucho” are a complete coincidence! Learn the history behind these and more.
body_markdown:
When you’re learning a new language, you want[all the help you can get](https://blog.duolingo.com/context-clues-while-traveling/) ! And while you may already know about[false cognates](https://blog.duolingo.com/false-cognates/) and[loanwords](https://blog.duolingo.com/how-loanwords-adapted-in-japanese/) that have taken on a different meaning, there’s another category of words whose looks can be deceiving: These 8 word pairs look alike *and* share the same meaning, but their histories are surprisingly separate!


**8 lookalike words to watch out for:**


- English much and Spanish mucho
- English island and French île
- Japanese emoji (絵文字) and English emoticon
- Spanish usted and Arabic 2ustaadh (أستاذ)
- Italian ciao and Vietnamese chào
- German Feuer and French feu
- Spanish dios and Greek theós (θεός)
- English have and Portuguese haver


## English *much* and Spanish *mucho*


**Both mean:** *much* , *a lot*
**The real story:** English and Spanish are both[Indo-European languages](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-families-overview/#indo-european) and they share[plenty of similar words](https://blog.duolingo.com/cognates-in-spanish/) . Usually, that means that the words came from the same source, but that isn’t the case for much


and mucho


! *Much* comes from Proto-Germanic (the ancestor language of English, German, and Dutch, among others) and looked like *myċel* in Old English, while mucho comes from the Latin *multus* .


## English *island* and French *île*


**Both mean:** *island*
**The real story:** This pair may be especially surprising if you know that English got[a lot of its vocabulary from French](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-english-language/#isn%E2%80%99t-english-a-romance-language) , or that the little hat on the “î” in île


, called a circumflex, often means that the word[used to have an “s”](https://blog.duolingo.com/french-accent-marks-pronunciation/#accent-circonflexe-%C3%A2-%C3%AA-%C3%AE-%C3%B4-%C3%BB) ! This means that *île* used to be spelled *isle* (where English gets the word isle


, too!), but it comes from the Latin *insula* , while island


comes from Old English *īeġland* . This means that even the similarities between the English words *island* and *isle* are a coincidence!


## Japanese *emoji* (絵文字) and English *emoticon*


**Both mean:** a text-based representation of moods or reactions
**The real story:** Who remembers when we were limited to expressing ourselves with the likes of ;) and :’( in our texts and emails? When[emoji became widespread](https://blog.duolingo.com/emoji-language-trends/) in the 2010s, many people mistakenly assumed that the words *emoji* (from Japanese 絵文字


) and emoticon


were related—but they aren’t! 絵文字 is made up of the characters 絵 (e), meaning picture, and 文字 (moji), meaning *character* , while *emoticon* is a[portmanteau](https://blog.duolingo.com/glamping-hangry-and-other-portmanteau-words/) of the words *emotion* and *icon* .


## Spanish *usted* and Arabic *2ustaadh* (أستاذ)


**Both are:** a way to show respect or formality
**The real story:** Even though they sound similar—and even though[Spanish has lots of influence from Arabic](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-spanish/) —these words have completely different histories: Usted


is a[pronoun](https://blog.duolingo.com/what-are-pronouns/) , and it comes from a shortened version of vuestra merced


, literally *your mercy* . Meanwhile, أستاذ


(2ustaadh) is an honorific title that comes from[Persian](https://blog.duolingo.com/are-arabic-hebrew-persian-related/) , where it originally meant *master* or *teacher* , and today it can be used to address university professors, or anyone who is a master in their field.


## Italian *ciao* and Vietnamese *chào*


**Both mean:** *hello* and *goodbye*
**The real story:** Not every language has a word that can function as a greeting **and** a farewell! But even though ciao


and chào


have this dual role in common and nearly-identical pronunciations, that’s where the similarities end: Italian *ciao* comes from a longer Venetian phrase, *s-ciào vostro* , meaning *I am your servant* ( *s-ciào* comes from Latin *sclavus* , meaning *slave* ), while Vietnamese *chào* is thought to come from the Chinese 朝


(cháo), which historically served as a greeting for elders or authority figures.


## German *Feuer* and French *feu*


**Both mean:** *fire*
**The real story:** German and French are both[Indo-European languages](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-families-overview/#indo-european) that have had lots of contact with each other for many, many centuries, so they do have plenty of words with shared histories—but not Feuer


and feu


! *Feuer* comes from Proto-Germanic, and looked like *fiur* in Old High German, and is related to English fire


. Meanwhile, *feu* came from Latin *focus* , which meant *hearth* !


## Spanish *dios* and Greek *theós* (θεός)


**Both mean:** *god*
**The real story:** Spanish—like all[Romance languages](https://blog.duolingo.com/what-are-romance-languages/) —comes from Latin, and Latin borrowed heavily from Ancient Greek, so it wouldn’t be too surprising for dios


and θεός


(theós) to have a shared history! Not only that, but anyone who’s familiar with Spanish pronunciation knows that the “d” sound is often pronounced a lot like a “th,” similar to the sound that “θ” (theta) makes. However, *dios* (along with the word *divine* ) both come from the Proto-Indo-European root **diew‑* , meaning *celestial* or *shining* , while θεός has been traced back to a different Proto-Indo-European root, **dhē‑* , which meant *to put* or *to place* .


## English *have* and Portuguese *haver*


**Both mean:** *to have*
**The real story:** English words have a long history of ending up in Romance languages and vice versa, so thinking that the similarities between have


and haver


are more than a coincidence would be a reasonable assumption! But *have* comes from a Proto-Indo-European word that meant *to seize* and probably looked like **habjaną* in Proto-Germanic, while *haver* can be traced back to an unrelated Latin word *habēre* , meaning *to grasp* . The same is true of German haben


and Spanish haber


, which also both mean *to have* and look suspiciously similar to each other, but while *haben* is related to *have* and *haber* is related to *haver* , *haben* and *haber* have no shared history with one another!


Confused? I don’t blame you! Here’s another way to visualize the way *have* , *haben* , *haber* , and *haver* evolved:


## Things aren’t always what they seem


Cognates and loanwords are an excellent way to boost your learning, but some words that look alike and share a similar meaning are just happy coincidences. But no matter how they got there, they’re still bonus vocabulary, and that means one less word you’ll have a hard time remembering! 😅
